To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) canopy openness has a strong effect on insect abundance and species richness in tropical forests; 2) the effect is mediated by changes in leaf production by trees, not by changes in microclimate; 3) the effect is species-specific, and the responses of most species are positive; 4) the responses are consistent with the prediction of the intermediate disturbance hypothesis; 5) the responses of most insect species are positive, suggesting that reduced impact logging may be beneficial to insect diversity

(i) canopy openness had no significant effect on insect abundance, diversity, or species composition, (ii) insect species richness increased after felling, (iii) most species increased in abundance after felling, but some declined, (iv) most species responded to changes in leaf production by the host plant, and (v) the integrity of the understorey insect community depends on minimizing damage to plants
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of canopy openness and leaf damage on the abundance and diversity of insect herbivorous species on five tree species in an un logged forest in Guyana, South America.
the effects of logging on the understorey fauna in a rain forest of Guyana.
the effects of logging on the insect fauna of a tropical forest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
canopy openness has little influence on insect herbivore abundance and species richness in tropical forests.
the canopy openness of 25% to 50% in the understoreys of tropical forests is not a major constraint on herbivore abundance and diversity.
the canopy opening caused by reduced impact logging in the rainforest studied here had a short term positive effect on the abundance of herbivores and a negative effect on their species richness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the integrity of insect herbivore communities in the under-storey depends more on minimizing the damage to the plant resources than on the canopy openness.
the effects of canopy opening on insect herbivore populations in the understoreys of wet tropical forests are highly variable and dependent on the plant species and insect taxa involved.

canopy openness is not an important determinant of insect diversity in the understoreys of tropical wet forest, but that canopy openness is an important determinant of the integrity of insect herbivore communities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of canopy openness depend on the plant resources that are available to the insects.
canopy disturbance can have profound effects on insect communities.
canopy openness is only one aspect of the disturbance process, and that the responses of insect communities to canopy openness depend on their feeding and microhabitat preferences.
